By Samantha Granville Beirut Published 3 hours ago Lebanon's parliament has voted to abolish the death penalty, a move that would make it the first country in the Middle East to formally end capital punishment. A majority of MPs in the 128-seat parliament backed the measure on Tuesday, while Hezbollah's parliamentary bloc voted against it. The legislation will now go to the cabinet before being passed to President Joseph Aoun for signing. The government has already expressed its support for the measure. Lebanon has not carried out an execution since January 2004, although courts have continued to hand down death sentences. Rights groups estimate that more than 78 people remain on death row. Under the new legislation, capital punishment will be replaced with life imprisonment with hard labour. However, the legislation does not yet set out in detail how the new sentence would be enforced. Hard labour is already written into Lebanese law but has rarely been implemented in recent years. The country's financial crisis and overcrowded prisons have limited the authorities' resources and capacity. The latest legislation follows years of campaigning by civil society groups and lawyers for the removal of capital punishment from Lebanese law. "We cannot solve a crime with a crime or end violence with violence," Oragit Younan told the BBC. As co-founder of the Lebanese Association for Civil Rights, she led a nearly three-decade campaign to abolish the death penalty in Lebanon. "We are in a war, and people [have been] killed every day, so even in this situation, we can fight, we can struggle for human rights, and we can win. We can be a model for others," she said. Tuesday's vote in parliament follows more than two decades of a de facto moratorium on executions. An execution required a decree signed by the president, prime minister and justice minister - but no such decree has been signed since 2004. Under Lebanese law, the death penalty could previously be imposed for some of the country's most serious offences, including aggravated murder, certain terrorism-related crimes resulting in death, treason, espionage and offences against state security. Previous attempts to abolish the death penalty have failed, including legislation introduced in parliament in 2004 and a proposal from the justice ministry in 2008. Lebanon's move comes as the use of the death penalty remains contested elsewhere in the Middle East. Jordan resumed executions in June, carrying out its first since 2017. In Israel, its parliament has approved legislation that allows for the expansion of the circumstances in which capital punishment can be imposed. Israeli MPs passed a new law in May to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for those involved in the Hamas-led attacks and mass hostage-taking in Israel in October 2023. Elsewhere, the UN human rights chief has said he is alarmed by the rise in executions in Iran, with capital punishment continuing to be used "to instil fear among the population and suppress dissent". In Iran, at least 56 people had been executed on national security-related charges since 19 March, including 27 in cases linked to January's nationwide anti-government protests, UN human rights chief Volker TÃ¼rk said earlier this month. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Breaking News Australia Australian Greens Jordon Steele-John says ‘I’m not on leave’ and accuses Greens leader of making ‘bad call’ regarding complaints Greens senator for WA says complaints regarding his behaviour towards women not about ‘accountability’ but rather ‘factionalism’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Sarah Basford Canales Sun 18 Oct 2026 10.51 BST Last modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 20.41 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jordon Steele-John has accused an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” and the leader, David Shoebridge, of pressuring him to take leave after complaints about his conduct were made public last week. The 32-year-old Greens senator released a six-page statement on Sunday night after Nine newspapers reported last week that seven former and current party members had demanded an investigation into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025. The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the Western Australian Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission . Steele-John said in the statement he wanted any alleged behaviour investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but claimed an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch had released the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate. Greens senator Jordon Steele-John takes leave amid investigation into complaints Read more “It is no coincidence that the letter arrived at the leader’s office the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection,” Steele-John said on Sunday. “It is my opinion that this is an attempt to influence forthcoming party preselections by deliberately leaking out of context or misleading information to smear potential candidates and myself.” Steele-John said some of the letter’s authors and signatories may have signed the letter out of “genuine commitment” to people who experienced violence but he was angry it had been politicised. “When processes meant to protect victims are turned into weapons in preselection contests, everyone loses. Survivors become less likely to be believed. Real complaints are treated with suspicion. And the people who did this know it,” he said. “That is not accountability. It is factionalism, and it has no place in the Greens.” The senator said he was not on leave, contrary to Shoebridge’s comments last week, and that he had been pressured by the leader to request leave on Thursday as Nine’s story was breaking. “I feel that he used those meetings to repeatedly pressure me to say that I would take leave,” Steele-John said. The senator said “survivors of family violence are entitled to make decisions about their own lives and the Greens have always said so”. “It was a bad call from David. We’ve all made those in politics. So, to be clear, I am not on leave and did not agree to the inclusion of that line within David’s statement.” Shoebridge said on Thursday that Steele-John had requested leave from the party room “and I have accepted it”. “Senator Steele-John has indicated to me that he’s on leave, and that leave means leave,” the Greens leader said on Friday. Guardian Australia contacted Shoebridge’s office for comment on Sunday night. Steele-John said the letter of complaint to Shoebridge referred to three matters but it did not set out any allegations in detail. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekdays Sign up to Afternoon Update Our Australian afternoon update breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Addressing a disparaging nickname – “feels on wheels” – the senator said he believed it originated because he was emotional during speeches early in his career regarding the disability royal commission. The nickname, however, had taken on a new meaning in recent time, he said in Sunday’s statement. “Over the years, this nickname would periodically resurface like strategic clockwork, growing in lore each time. “Eventually, I was informed that this phrase, which mocked my disability and my emotions, had taken on a new, more sinister meaning: that I had treated women inappropriately.” Steele-John said another matter contained in the letter related to alleged sexual harassment at a Greens campaign party in 2024; however, the authors did not outline specific allegations. The senator said the final matter related to alleged “serious sexual misconduct”. An investigation into alleged sexual assault was ultimately closed by the Western Australian police with a finding of no charges, he said. Comment was sought from WA police. “It took people close to me to make me realise that I was experiencing domestic violence,” Steele-John said in Sunday’s statement. Nine last week reported on the existence of a 47-page “secret dossier”, first drafted in 2016 , which the newspaper said contained allegations against Steele-John and how the party should respond if they were to come to light. Steele-John said on Sunday he had an “interpersonal conflict” between himself and two friends in 2016 before he was preselected. The senator alleged the unofficial faction had attempted to shop the “half-heard rumours” of the conflict to journalists in 2017 as part of a “smear campaign”. As a result, Steele-John said, the document was created so the party office and staff had “the same accurate information to give anyone who had heard the rumours and was concerned”.
